techniques.name: AI Model Poisoning via MCP Tool Training Data Contamination
techniques.description: Attackers contaminate training data used to develop AI models for MCP tools, implanting backdoors that activate during specific conditions

techniques.name: Tool Poisoning Attack (TPA)
techniques.description: Attackers embed malicious instructions within MCP tool descriptions that are invisible to users but processed by LLMs. This technique exploits the difference between the displayed tool description and the description processed by the AI model.

attackVectors.primary: Malicious tool description injection through compromised MCP servers
secondary: Supply chain compromise of legitimate MCP tool packages
Social engineering to convince users to install poisoned tools
Exploitation of tool marketplace/registry vulnerabilities
Full-Schema Poisoning (FSP): Poisoning entire tool schemas beyond descriptions
MCP Rug Pulls: Deploying legitimate tools that later update to include malicious definitions

subTechniques.name: Description-Based Poisoning
subTechniques.description: Hidden instructions in tool descriptions via HTML comment injection, Unicode character exploitation, Bidirectional text manipulation

subTechniques.name: Full-Schema Poisoning (FSP)
subTechniques.description: Extending attacks beyond descriptions to entire tool schemas including parameter names, types, defaults, and enum values

subTechniques.name: Output Poisoning
subTechniques.description: Manipulating tool outputs to inject instructions for subsequent LLM processing via structured output injection, markdown exploitation, multi-stage attacks

subTechniques.name: Dynamic Poisoning (Rug Pulls)
subTechniques.description: Time-delayed or conditional activation of malicious behavior including time-bomb activation, usage-based triggers, and remote control

subTechniques.name: Cross-Tool Poisoning
subTechniques.description: Exploiting interactions between multiple tools via chain attacks, permission escalation, and context pollution

realWorldIncidents: Gmail Message Exploit in Claude Desktop (July 2025)

techniques.name: Supply Chain Compromise
techniques.description: Distribution of backdoored MCP server packages through unofficial repositories or compromised legitimate sources. Attackers infiltrate the software distribution pipeline to inject malicious code into MCP servers before they reach end users.

attackVectors.primary: Compromised package repositories distributing backdoored MCP servers
secondary: Typosquatting attacks targeting popular MCP server names
Compromised developer accounts with publishing access
Man-in-the-middle attacks during package installation
Social engineering targeting package maintainers
Dependency confusion attacks in monorepo environments

techniques.name: Malicious MCP-Server Distribution
techniques.description: Adversary ships a trojanized server package or Docker image that users install, gaining foothold when the host registers its tools. This technique differs from supply chain compromise in that attackers create entirely new malicious packages.

attackVectors.primary: Direct distribution of malicious MCP servers disguised as legitimate tools
secondary: Social media promotion of malicious MCP tools
GitHub repositories with malicious MCP server implementations
Docker Hub images containing backdoored MCP servers
Marketplace listings for fake MCP integrations
Forum posts and blog articles promoting malicious tools

techniques.name: Server Impersonation / Name-Collision
techniques.description: Attacker registers a server with the same name/URL as a trusted one, or hijacks discovery, so the client connects to them instead. Exploits weaknesses in naming and discovery systems (DNS, mDNS, local MCP server registries).

attackVectors.primary: Malicious server registration with a trusted server's name or identifier
secondary: DNS cache poisoning or DNS hijacking
Rogue DHCP infrastructure distributing attacker-controlled DNS settings
Duplicate local registry entries for existing trusted server
TLS certificate misuse, weak validation, or certificate pinning gaps
ARP spoofing on local networks
Service redeployment windows where identity checks are temporarily bypassed

techniques.name: Exposed Endpoint Exploit
techniques.description: Misconfigured public MCP endpoints (no auth, debug on) let attackers connect, enumerate tools or trigger RCE. Covers both public/LAN exposure and browser-to-localhost attacks via DNS rebinding or Cross-Site WebSocket Hijacking.

attackVectors.primary: Network-accessible MCP servers without proper authentication
secondary: Localhost HTTP/SSE/WebSocket servers without origin validation
DNS rebinding attacks against localhost MCP servers
Docker container port mapping exposing MCP servers
Reverse tunneling tools inadvertently exposing MCP servers

techniques.name: User-Social-Engineering Install
techniques.description: Phishing/social posts persuade developers to install a seemingly legitimate package or installer which silently registers dangerous capabilities with MCP.

attackVectors.primary: Phishing / Social Engineering targeting developers or operators
secondary: Registry Poisoning / Typosquatting
Supply-Chain Compromise of legitimate tool repositories
Compromised Installer distribution

techniques.name: OAuth Authorization Phishing
techniques.description: Malicious MCP servers exploit OAuth flows to steal access tokens from legitimate services by tricking users during authorization. The malicious server captures OAuth tokens, granting attackers access to user accounts on third-party services.

attackVectors.primary: Malicious MCP server configuration through user deception
secondary: Social engineering to promote malicious server URLs
Typosquatting on popular MCP server names
Compromised documentation or tutorials containing malicious server URLs
Supply chain attacks on MCP server registries

techniques.name: Tool Shadowing Attack
techniques.description: Malicious MCP servers impersonate or interfere with legitimate tools to hijack execution within MCP-based workflows through cross-server tool interference. Exploits the fact that MCP allows AI agents to connect to multiple tool servers simultaneously.

attackVectors.primary: Cross-server tool interference through malicious tool descriptions
secondary: Tool impersonation with similar names and metadata
Confused deputy attacks
Description-based hijacking through embedded instructions
Silent tool redefinition (rug pulls)
Cross-origin tool invocation

techniques.name: Authorization Server Mix-up
techniques.description: Client follows redirect to look-alike AS domain (e.g., accounts-google.com vs accounts.google.com), causing authorization codes or tokens to be leaked to attacker-controlled server.

attackVectors.primary: Typosquatted or homograph domains mimicking legitimate Authorization Servers
secondary: Malicious MCP server configurations redirecting to attacker-controlled AS
Compromised OAuth discovery metadata
Man-in-the-middle attacks manipulating authorization redirects
DNS hijacking or DNS cache poisoning targeting OAuth endpoints
International Domain Name (IDN) homograph attacks

techniques.name: Command Injection
techniques.description: Exploitation of unsanitized input in MCP server implementations leading to remote code execution. Attackers exploit the direct incorporation of user-supplied input into system commands without proper sanitization.

attackVectors.primary: Direct command injection through unsanitized parameters in MCP tool calls
secondary: Prompt injection attacks manipulating AI agents to call tools with malicious payloads
Supply chain compromise through forked vulnerable MCP server implementations
Option injection through filenames or parameters starting with dash
SSRF to credential theft/RCE via internal services

techniques.name: Prompt Injection (Multiple Vectors)
techniques.description: Malicious instructions injected through various vectors to manipulate AI behavior via MCP

techniques.name: Fake Tool Invocation (Function Spoofing)
techniques.description: Adversary forges JSON that mimics an MCP function-call message, tricking the host into running a tool that was never offered

techniques.name: Over-Privileged Tool Abuse
techniques.description: Legit tool (e.g. Shell) runs with broader OS rights than necessary; LLM can be induced to perform arbitrary commands

techniques.name: Path Traversal via File Tool
techniques.description: File-handling tool accepts relative paths like ../../secret.key; attacker leaks host secrets

techniques.name: Autonomous Loop Exploit
techniques.description: Craft prompts that push an agent into infinite self-invoke loop to exhaust CPU or hit rate limits (DoS)

techniques.name: Debugging Tool Exploitation
techniques.description: Browser-based remote code execution via vulnerable MCP Inspector (CVE-2025-49596)

techniques.name: Multimodal Prompt Injection via Images/Audio
techniques.description: Embedding malicious instructions within image or audio content to manipulate multimodal AI behavior

techniques.name: AI Agent CLI Weaponization
techniques.description: Malicious exploitation of AI coding assistant CLI tools with dangerous flags for reconnaissance and data exfiltration

techniques.name: MCP Rug Pull Attack
techniques.description: Time-delayed malicious tool definition changes after initial approval. Tools function legitimately initially then silently change behavior.

techniques.name: OAuth Token Persistence

techniques.name: Backdoored Server Binary
techniques.description: Inserts cron job or reverse shell on install; persists even if MCP service is uninstalled

techniques.name: Context Memory Implant
techniques.description: Malicious agent writes itself into long-term vector store; re-loaded in every future session

techniques.name: Persistent Tool Redefinition
techniques.description: Attacker modifies server's tool metadata to keep hidden commands across restarts

techniques.name: Credential Implant in Config
techniques.description: Adds attacker's API/SSH keys to server .env, giving re-entry

techniques.name: Hijack Update Mechanism
techniques.description: Man-in-the-middle an auto-update channel to re-install malicious build later on

techniques.name: Context Memory Poisoning via Vector Store Contamination
techniques.description: Attackers manipulate vector databases storing long-term memory for AI agents, creating persistent malicious content that contaminates knowledge across all future sessions

techniques.name: Cross-Server Tool Shadowing
techniques.description: Malicious MCP servers override legitimate tool calls to gain elevated privileges

techniques.name: High-Privilege Tool Abuse
techniques.description: Invoke a VM-level or root tool from normal user context

techniques.name: Sandbox Escape via Server Exec
techniques.description: Exploit vulnerable server to break container/seccomp isolation

techniques.name: Credential Relay Chain
techniques.description: Use one tool to steal tokens, feed them to second tool with higher privileges

techniques.name: Host OS Priv-Esc (RCE)
techniques.description: Achieve root via misconfigured service running as root, then alter host

techniques.name: Rogue Authorization Server
techniques.description: Malicious MCP server redirects OAuth flows to attacker-controlled AS that ignores audience restrictions and Proof of Possession (PoP), minting overly-permissive super-tokens with expanded scopes

techniques.name: Confused Deputy Attack
techniques.description: MCP server receives token for one user (Alice) and forwards it to another user's (Bob) MCP instance, allowing Bob to perform actions as Alice by exploiting the server's trusted position

techniques.name: Token Scope Substitution
techniques.description: Attacker swaps a limited-scope token with one that has broader permissions but same audience, exploiting insufficient scope validation to gain elevated privileges

techniques.name: Privileged Tool Invocation via Prompt Manipulation
techniques.description: Adversary manipulates MCP agent prompts to bypass safety rules and invoke privileged tools

techniques.name: Line Jumping
techniques.description: Bypassing security checkpoints through context injection before tool invocation

techniques.name: Instruction Steganography
techniques.description: Zero-width chars/HTML comments hide directives in tool metadata

techniques.name: Consent-Fatigue Exploit
techniques.description: Repeated benign prompts desensitize user; crucial request hidden mid-flow

techniques.name: Response Tampering
techniques.description: Model instructed not to mention risky action, keeping UI output harmless

techniques.name: Tool Obfuscation/Renaming

techniques.name: Metadata Manipulation

techniques.name: Server Proxy Masquerade
techniques.description: Malicious server silently proxies legit API so traffic looks normal in network logs

techniques.name: OAuth Protocol Downgrade
techniques.description: Attacker forces use of less secure OAuth 2.0 implicit flow instead of authorization code flow, bypassing PKCE protections and enabling easier token theft

techniques.name: Full-Schema Poisoning (FSP)
techniques.description: Exploitation of entire MCP tool schema beyond descriptions for credential theft

techniques.name: File-Based Credential Harvest
techniques.description: Use file tools to read SSH keys, cloud creds

techniques.name: Env-Var Scraping

techniques.name: Token Theft via API Response

techniques.name: In-Memory Secret Extraction

techniques.name: Infrastructure Token Theft

techniques.name: Authorization Code Interception

techniques.name: Directory Listing via File Tool

techniques.name: API Data Harvest

techniques.name: Covert Channel in Responses

mitigations.name: Control/Data Flow Separation
mitigations.description: Implementing control/data flow separation through systems like CaMeL provides provable security against prompt injection by ensuring untrusted tool descriptions cannot influence program execution

mitigations.name: Cryptographic Integrity for Tool Descriptions
mitigations.description: Tool descriptions should be cryptographically hashed and signed by trusted authorities, with signature verification before loading

mitigations.name: AI-Powered Content Analysis
mitigations.description: Deploy LLM-based systems to analyze tool descriptions for semantic anomalies and hidden instructions before they reach production systems

mitigations.name: Unicode Sanitization and Filtering
mitigations.description: Implement filtering for Private Use Area characters, Bidirectional control characters, and all non-essential Unicode characters from untrusted sources

mitigations.name: Content Sanitization
mitigations.description: Filter tool descriptions to remove hidden content and instruction patterns. Note: pattern-based filtering alone is insufficient

mitigations.name: Tool Registry Verification
mitigations.description: Install MCP servers only from verified sources with cryptographic signatures

mitigations.name: Content Rendering Parity

mitigations.name: Visual Validation
